newsitem.title: USA: New England states' rebound starts accelerating.
newsitem.headline: New England states' rebound starts accelerating.

text.p: New England states, which suffered severe downturns in the early 1990s even though the national recession was fairly mild, began turning the corner last year and now are gaining momentum, state officials said this week.
While the bruises have healed, the officials, who spoke at at Bond Buyer conference here on New England public finance, were candid about the widespread impact the recession had.
Many shifted to finding jobs for their residents in financial services and high technology as manufacturing and defense, once the mainsprings of their economies, retrenched.
As these industries cutback and state revenues fell, governors slashed spending and many are still trying to cut more out of their budgets in the next couple of years.

For example, Maine, which faces a $420 million shortfall for its next two-year budget, which runs from 1998 to 1999, plans to reduce spending by $65 million, after slashing its last two-year budget by $45 million.
Several of the states, like Vermont and Massachusetts, have greatly reduced their short-term borrowing, and improved their cash positions, which also have benefited from an upturn in revenues.
Noting that revenues were running right on target, James Douglas, Vermont state treasurer, said, "We're much stabler than we were a year ago."
Ken Olshansky, deputy treasurer of Massachusetts, noted that the state's unemployment rate has droped to 4.5 percent from 9.6 percent in 1991.

"We've had dramatic improvements in our cash position," he said, adding that the state last week decided it did not need to go ahead with a $500 million note sale planned for this month because it had money in the bank.

Many of the state officials partly attributed their rebounds to efforts to make their states more attractive to businesses, by cutting workers' compensation programs, using special tax credits, and investing in colleges and industrial parks.
And some state officials do not long for the heady, high-growth rates that preceeded the recession.
Georgie Thomas, the treasurer for New Hampshire, noting the real estate sector was growing at a moderate pace, added "We like that because it's sustainable."
The rebound in the New England economies also has left the states much better prepared if there is another downturn, or if job growth stalls.

"In Connecticut, we're looking for a slow, steady climb after this big trough we've been in so I don't think we'd have to change our game plan much at all," said David Warren an official with the state Treasurer's office.

While the state saw the two main pillars of its economy, defence and the insurance and financial sectors, crumble at the same time, it has gained 65,000 jobs since late 1992, Warren said. "Most of the growth is in retail, trade and services, but a lot of the growth we see is in small businesses," he said.
Despite the new emphasis on high-technology firms, financial services and small business, manufacturing remains an important part of at least some of the state's economies.

Although the number of manufacturing jobs has fallen sharply, with Rhode Island's share falling to 85,000 from 128,000 in 1990, the sector still makes up about the same 20 to 25 percent of the state's economy.

Jim Thorsen, an official with the Rhode Island state Treasury office, explained that that is because the manufacuring jobs that have stayed mainly have been ones that require highly skilled workers. That is one of the reason's Rhode Island voters will be asked on the November ballot to approve selling about $33 million of bonds to modernize the state's university system.
Rhode Island hopes these sorts of investments will help it prepare its residents for employers who require their workers to have technical skills.
